articles.headline: Treasury Sanctions Iranian Oil Traders and Government Insiders for Alleged Oil Revenue Scheme
body: The U.S. Treasury Department announced new sanctions against Iranian oil traders and government-linked facilitators on Friday, accusing them of assisting Tehran in selling oil abroad and illicitly profiting from the revenues. This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast' and was imposed under two executive orders targeting Iran's petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, as well as a counterterrorism authority.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated that 'Iran's tyrannical regime never fails to put its own interests before those of its own citizens, even as ordinary Iranians face shortages of bread and fuel.' The department claims that no oil has been loaded onto vessels since the operation began, and none is currently on the water outside the U.S. military blockade imposed during the ongoing war.

Among those designated are Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) intelligence officer, and Majid Taj, brother of the head of the Iranian Football Federation, who are accused of leading a network selling oil from Iran's dwindling reserves. Mohammadhossein Servati, son of IRGC Brig. Gen. Mohsen Servati, and Mojtaba Arabnejad, son of Mahan Air CEO Hamid Arabnejad, were also sanctioned.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Cuba Frequently Asked Questions Amidst Expanded Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba, coinciding with recent expanded U.S. sanctions targeting the Cuban economy. These FAQs aim to provide clarity on the implementation and scope of the updated measures.

The new guidance comes as the U.S. continues its 'maximum pressure' campaign against Cuba, which has included fuel-shipping sanctions, tanker designations, and remittance restrictions. These measures have been criticized for exacerbating Cuba's humanitarian crisis and placing additional barriers on access to essential goods and services.

The United Nations General Assembly has consistently adopted resolutions calling for the termination of the U.S. embargo against Cuba, a position reaffirmed in 2026, highlighting international opposition to unilateral coercive measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals in Counter Narcotics and Cyber-related Actions, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under its counter narcotics and cyber-related sanctions programs. This action targets individuals involved in illicit drug trafficking and cyber activities, aiming to disrupt transnational criminal organizations.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued Illicit Drugs General License 1, which authorizes a wind-down period for transactions involving certain persons blocked on November 19, 2026. This license provides a limited timeframe for legitimate transactions to conclude.

Additionally, OFAC issued Russia-related General License 131L, authorizing certain transactions for the negotiation and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH, along with related maintenance activities. Two associated, amended Frequently Asked Questions, FAQs 1224 and 1225, were also released to provide further guidance.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under its counter terrorism sanctions program. These actions target individuals and entities identified as supporting terrorist activities globally. The specific details of the designated parties were not immediately released in a public statement but are reflected in updates to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

These designations underscore the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to disrupting financial networks that facilitate terrorism and protecting the international financial system from illicit activities.
Entities and individuals added to the SDN list are subject to asset blocking, and U.S. persons are generally prohibited from engaging in transactions with them.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting several Guatemalan drug trafficking organizations for their involvement in both counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. This action aims to disrupt the financial and operational networks of these groups.

Among the entities added to OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List are LOS LORENZANAS (also known as LORENZANA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION, 'THE LORENZANA CLAN,' and 'THE LORENZANA FAMILY'), LOS MENDOZA DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION, and LOS HUISTAS DRUG TRAFFICKING ORGANIZATION. These groups are identified as criminal organizations with links to Mexican narco-terrorist cartels like the Sinaloa Cartel and Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion (CJNG).
These designations carry secondary sanctions risks under Executive Order 13224, as amended by Executive Order 13886, further isolating these organizations from the international financial system.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has released an update to its Iran designation list. While specific details of the update were not immediately provided in the announcement, such actions typically involve adding new individuals or entities to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List or modifying existing entries.

These updates are part of the ongoing U.S. strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran, particularly targeting sectors and individuals perceived to be supporting the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities.
Multinational corporations and financial institutions are advised to regularly check OFAC's updated lists to ensure compliance and avoid potential penalties for engaging in prohibited transactions.

articles.headline: U.S. Sanctions Cripple Financial Networks Sustaining the Iranian Regime
body: The U.S. Treasury Department announced a new round of Iran-related designations, targeting financial networks accused of sustaining the Iranian regime. This action is part of a broader effort to cut off revenue streams that Washington claims Iran uses to finance its military capabilities and destabilize the region.
These measures follow previous actions under 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which aims to intensify pressure on Iran by expanding sector-based sanctions and narrowing licensing options.
The designations include eight Canada-based money services businesses, highlighting the U.S. government's focus on disrupting illicit financial flows globally that benefit the Iranian regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Imposes New Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting cyber-related actors and transnational criminal organizations. This action aims to combat illicit activities that pose threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

Concurrently, OFAC has imposed new sanctions on Cuba, including designations and the publication of a Cuba-related determination. These measures extend Executive Order 14404 to four additional sectors of the Cuban economy: manufacturing, technology, electronics, and marine.

The new Cuba sanctions also include designations of Cuban oil shippers, Cuban state entities, and Chinese military suppliers, specifically China National Electronic Import and Export Company (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies Co., Ltd., for materially assisting the Government of Cuba.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Fraudulent Ship Registries and Aviation Support for Iranian Regime, Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, targeting fraudulent ship registries and entities providing aviation support to the Iranian regime. These actions are part of a broader U.S. effort to disrupt Iran's ability to generate revenue and support its illicit activities.
The Treasury Department also updated certain Iran-related listings and published an Iran-related OFAC Alert, signaling heightened vigilance against attempts to circumvent sanctions.
In a separate development, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question, providing updated guidance for transactions involving Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. While the specific details of the amendments were not immediately disclosed, such changes typically modify the scope of authorized transactions or activities with Iran.
This amendment comes amidst a period of intensified U.S. sanctions pressure on Iran, with a focus on expanding sector-based sanctions and narrowing existing licensing options.
Businesses and individuals engaged in Iran-related activities are advised to review the amended General License carefully to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo-related Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting entities and individuals related to North Korea. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programs and other illicit activities.

Concurrently, OFAC also issued designations related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. These measures aim to address issues such as human rights abuses, corruption, and destabilizing activities within the region.
These designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to using sanctions as a tool to promote international peace and security, and to hold accountable those who undermine these objectives.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,529,685 for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations (URSR). The violations occurred between September 2018 and March 2022.

The apparent violations stemmed from Extreme Networks exporting networking equipment and related services to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by the designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey, even though MMZA itself was not independently listed on the SDN List until 2022.

OFAC determined that the violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement amount reflects these factors, with the company's U.S.-led compliance team having reviewed the purchase agreement but failing to conduct sufficient due diligence to identify MMZA as a blocked entity.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 to OFAC for 475 Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle 475 apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs. This settlement was part of a coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering failures.

The apparent violations, occurring between September 2021 and April 2025, involved transactions totaling approximately $14.8 million across sanctions programs related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. OFAC categorized the violations as non-egregious and mostly not voluntarily disclosed.

Key factors contributing to the violations included delayed updates to sanctions screening filters, analyst errors, and an alert suppression rule, particularly concerning blocked banks listed in a third-party vendor's payment routing directory.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015 Over Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle its potential civil liability for apparent violations of OFAC counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations. The violations involved arranging the shipment of equipment from a designated Chinese supplier.

The apparent violations occurred when Pegasus arranged for the import of a sugar packet-filling machine from Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., a Chinese supplier designated under Executive Order 14059 for selling pill presses to counterfeit-pill makers. Youli had changed its name after designation, and Pegasus only screened the new name, missing the SDN-listed identifiers.

OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed. The settlement also addressed Pegasus's initial failure to fully respond to an administrative subpoena, highlighting the importance of thorough screening and complete cooperation with OFAC inquiries.

articles.headline: Individual Pays $1,427,230 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. The specific details of the individual's violations were not immediately released in a public statement but are outlined in the settlement agreement.
This enforcement action underscores OFAC's commitment to holding individuals accountable for non-compliance with sanctions laws, regardless of their affiliation with corporate entities.
The penalty amount reflects OFAC's assessment of the severity of the violations and other factors, including whether the conduct was voluntarily self-disclosed and deemed egregious.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $60,764 for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer of weighing equipment, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle its and its Italian subsidiary's potential civil liability for eight apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran. The violations occurred when its Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported goods to Iran through a distributor in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

Between July 2019 and November 2021, Dini Argeo S.r.l. exported weighing equipment to a UAE distributor with the knowledge that these goods would be reexported to an end-user in Iran. This occurred despite Rice Lake having instructed its subsidiary to cease sales to Iran after the revocation of General License H in 2018.

OFAC held Rice Lake responsible for its subsidiary's violations, emphasizing that companies cannot indirectly conduct prohibited activities. The case highlights the importance of robust oversight of foreign subsidiaries and distributors in high-risk jurisdictions.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Pays $1,050,000 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: FTI Consulting, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. The specific details of the violations were not immediately released in a public statement but are outlined in the settlement agreement.

This enforcement action demonstrates OFAC's continued focus on ensuring compliance across various industries, including professional services firms, which may inadvertently engage in transactions with sanctioned parties.
The penalty amount reflects OFAC's assessment of the case, considering factors such as the nature of the violations, the company's cooperation, and any remedial measures implemented.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Settles with OFAC for $275,000,000
body: Adani Enterprises Limited, an Indian multinational conglomerate, has agreed to pay a substantial penalty of $275,000,000 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. The specific details of the violations were not immediately released in a public statement but are outlined in the settlement agreement.
This significant penalty underscores OFAC's global reach and its commitment to enforcing U.S. sanctions against foreign entities, particularly those operating in critical sectors.
The large settlement amount reflects the gravity of the apparent violations and serves as a strong deterrent for other international companies to ensure strict adherence to U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Pays $1,110,661 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle potential civil liability for apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations. The specific details of the violations were not immediately released in a public statement but are outlined in the settlement agreement.

This enforcement action highlights OFAC's scrutiny of financial institutions and brokerage firms to ensure they have robust compliance programs in place to prevent transactions with sanctioned individuals or entities.
The penalty amount reflects OFAC's assessment of the violations, including factors such as the nature and extent of the prohibited transactions, and the company's efforts to remediate the issues.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $3,777,000 for Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: A U.S. citizen residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations. The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021.
This significant penalty against an individual underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions against those who engage in prohibited transactions, even when operating outside the United States.
The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination of the egregious nature of the violations and the individual's knowledge of the prohibited activities.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Pays $1,720,000 to OFAC for Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a U.S.-based academic and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle apparent violations of the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations. The violations involved entering into tuition enrollment agreements and processing payments for individuals designated under the Kingpin Act.

Over a five-year period, IMG Academy processed 89 financial transactions, including wire transfers and credit card payments, for the benefit of the children of two individuals designated under the Kingpin Act due to their ties to a sanctioned Mexican drug cartel.

OFAC found that routine due diligence, such as screening contracting parties or payors, would have revealed that the individuals' names matched entries on the SDN List. The case highlights that academic institutions, despite often perceiving themselves as low-risk, face significant sanctions exposure due to international student bodies and foreign payors.

articles.headline: U.S. Urges Singapore and Malaysia to Intensify Iran Sanctions Enforcement
body: U.S. Treasury officials have reportedly urged authorities in Singapore and Malaysia to increase scrutiny of companies potentially acting on behalf of Iranian interests. These discussions, held on November 20, 2026, involved regulators and national security bodies and focused on maritime transport, aviation services, and procurement.

Reuters reported that the U.S. is also encouraging banks and law firms operating in the two Southeast Asian nations to remain vigilant. The renewed attention highlights the challenges firms face in identifying beneficial ownership in complex transactions, particularly when registered company names obscure the ultimate beneficiaries.

Both Singapore and Malaysia implement UN Security Council sanctions on Iran, with Singapore's Monetary Authority providing guidance on applicable instruments. However, OFAC designations can arise under additional U.S. authorities, requiring a separate analysis for each transaction.

articles.headline: U.S. Sanctions Four Iranians Over Proceeds from Overseas Oil Sales
body: The U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions on Friday against four Iranians, accusing them of facilitating Tehran's evasion of U.S. sanctions by collecting and transferring revenue from overseas oil sales. The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) added these individuals to its sanctions list for their roles in operations designed to circumvent U.S. financial restrictions.

These measures freeze the designated individuals' property and interests in property within the United States or held or controlled by U.S. persons. U.S. individuals and companies are generally prohibited from transacting with them, and foreign financial institutions risk U.S. sanctions if they knowingly conduct or facilitate significant transactions on their behalf.
This action is part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which Washington initiated on August 24 to cut off revenue it asserts Iran uses to finance its military capabilities and ongoing war efforts.

articles.headline: BIS Restricts Remote Access to Advanced AI Chips, Rescinds AI Diffusion Rule
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued an interim final rule (IFR) amending the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to restrict remote access to advanced AI semiconductors. The rule, effective immediately upon publication in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026, targets data centers outside the United States that provide significant computing power to companies headquartered in China and other countries of concern.

The IFR formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule and imposes new destination-based license requirements for exports, reexports, or in-country transfers of advanced computing items to five additional countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil. BIS cites a high risk of diversion to China from these nations.

A new end-use-based license requirement is also established for advanced computing items destined for non-U.S. data centers that provide remote access to a 'significant volume of compute power' to end users headquartered in Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination (including China). This aims to prevent circumvention of existing restrictions through remote computing arrangements.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce BIS / Federal Register

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
